text.approach: Start at the Cold Springs trailhead (about 5,600 ft) at the end of FR 8040 and walk the South Climb Trail up the old roadbed to its junction with the Round the Mountain Trail near 6,200 ft. Turn right (northwest) onto the Round the Mountain Trail and follow its up-and-down traverse for roughly two miles, much of it under snow in early season, to the stream draining the Avalanche Glacier basin near 6,100 ft. Follow the stream and the moraines above it to the moraine-filled bowl at about 7,200 ft, where the Avalanche Glacier route and the Southwest Chutes meet. The glacier begins above this bowl, and a camp here shortens the summit day.
text.overview: Approach via the PCT or the Shorthorn trail. Under normal conditions, climb the glacier on its right side. Parties go in late spring; expect mostly moderate to steep snow, sometimes with a headwall of alpine ice. Simul-climbing works for most of it, and pickets with a running belay give protection if needed. Descend by the south side or the neighboring snowfield.
text.descent: Climb out onto the summit plateau and head for the true summit, then descend the South Spur: cross the crater rim past Pikers Peak and follow the broad snow slopes of Crescent Ridge down to the Lunch Counter flats, where glissading is common on soft snow. text.approach: A free wilderness permit is self-issued at the trailhead. From the Riley Camp Trailhead, hike the Riley Camp Trail, staying off the Riley Cut-Off at the first junction, until it meets the Pacific Crest Trail. Turn south on the Pacific Crest Trail for a few minutes to Riley Creek and follow the creek up through boulders to the moraines at the foot of the Pinnacle Glacier. The headwall route begins at the base of the glacier.
text.approach_logistics: {"trailhead":"Riley Camp Trailhead","trailheadDirection":"From Trout Lake, drive Mt. Adams Road north about 1.3 miles, then turn left onto Forest Road 23 (Buck Creek Road) and follow it about 17.5 miles to the trailhead, which is easy to miss between mileposts 38 and 37."}
text.overview: At the base the line may be obvious or not; several variations exist, so pick one. No cracks are on the route. The angle is mild at first and steep near the top. Rock bands seem stable, so objective danger looks modest. The route ends on the Pinnacle summit, an easy stroll from the main summit. Descend along the West Ridge; some parts are exposed though easy.

text.approach: Drive the Harts Pass road over the pass and down the Slate Creek road to the locked gate (about 3,800 ft). Walk the old South Fork Slate Creek road roughly a mile to the large bridge near 4,000 ft, then leave the road and travel south through open forest.
text.overview: The approach most climbers use: a bushwhack from the Slate Creek road to the east ridge, a steep vegetated slot, scrambling into the east cirque, then a ledge traverse to the summit gully on the west side of the top block.
text.descent: Retrace the route; descend the green slot carefully and keep to the forest on the left on the way down to avoid the alder.

text.approach: Shares the same general approach drainage as the West Route (Jug Creek/Bluff Lake/Cliff Lake benches) to gain the west side of the mountain, then continues around/up to the base of the north ridge rather than the west-ridge saddle system.

text.overview: A roughly 1,500-ft alpine rock route up Chaval's north ridge: mostly moderate 3rd/4th-class scrambling on solid, well-fractured granitic rock, with two harder pitches on the steepest section near the top.
text.descent: Parties commonly traverse off the summit and descend the West Route's ramp/heather line rather than downclimbing the North Ridge.

text.approach: Approach is up a brush-choked valley low in the Goodell Creek drainage — rough enough that even seasoned Cascades climbers have balked at it. This is the opposite (northeast) side of the peak from the standard Triumph Pass/Despair Lakes approach.
text.overview: A ~3,700 ft previously-unclimbed buttress line up Mt. Despair's northeast side to its north summit, opened in 2014: an easy 5.6 opening corner, a series of notches requiring short rappels, a stout 5.9 pitch through a deep summit-area cleft, a further steep pitch to the north ridge, and a snow-ridge finish.
text.descent: From the north summit, the first-ascent party exited over Triumph Pass and out the Thornton Lakes Trail rather than retracing the Goodell Creek approach.

text.approach: From the Necklace Valley Trailhead, follow the Necklace Valley Trail up the East Fork Foss River, over the river crossing and the steep climb beyond it, to the hanging valley holding La Bohn Lakes, where parties camp. From the lakes, climb the snow chute or talus to La Bohn Gap; the climb proper heads due north from the gap toward the summit.
